name: Oromo
subtitle: Oromo: who the sources name, where they live, and what the old labels got wrong.

keyPoints.text: In the 2007 census Afaan Oromo was the largest mother tongue in Ethiopia (33.8%), ahead of Amharic (29.3%); in 1994 Amharic had been largest.
Afaan Oromo is written in the Latin alphabet, while Amharic and Tigrigna use Ge'ez script (regional states chose scripts freely).

parts.text: In the 2007 census Afaan Oromo was the largest mother tongue in Ethiopia (33.8%), ahead of Amharic (29.3%); in 1994 Amharic had been largest.

image.caption: The Bale Mountains, in Ethiopia's Oromia region.

parts.text: Afaan Oromo is written in the Latin alphabet, while Amharic and Tigrigna use Ge'ez script (regional states chose scripts freely).
Four regional languages including Afaan Oromo were elevated to federal working-language status alongside Amharic (announced late February 2020).
Before 2020 the federal working language was Amharic only; the 2015 article describes 'federal monolingualism' with regional language autonomy. Oromia's working language is Afan Oromo.
Oromia is the largest regional state in Ethiopia by population and territory; a 2017 estimate gave more than 40 million inhabitants, including non-Oromo residents (Amhara about 7.2%).

The Oromo are described as living in the highlands alongside Amhara and Tigray; the LoC study (1991 edition) gave them about 40 percent of the population (an older, higher estimate than the 2007 census).
Gadaa is a generational class system typical of the Oromo in Ethiopia and Kenya, with promotions at fixed eight-year intervals (brief mention only).
Gadaa described as a system of generation classes succeeding each other every eight years (second source).

The name 'Galla' was the Amhara name for the Oromo in the LoC study's wording; an academic article (Kumsa 2019) discusses it in the context of dehumanising Abyssinian texts and quotes Bale resistance material objecting to 'filthy Galla'. No readable source states outright that 'many Oromo reject it' in neutral wording.
Asafa Jalata's view (quoted by Meressa 2019, attributed not asserted): the Oromo were conquered by and absorbed into Ethiopia in the nineteenth century.
Meressa 2019 notes the Oromo Liberation Front has struggled for independence since the early 1970s without achieving its stated objective (his wording; contested politics).

Identity and 1995 federalism: the Oromia regional constitution is described as an instrument of self-rule for the Oromo people (Disasa), and Meressa notes the 1995 constitution recognised nations' self-determination.
Critics of ethnic federalism (Midega's summary of one perspective): accuse the EPRDF of dividing the country along ethnic and linguistic lines and favour geographical federalism.

items.text: Oromo groups moved in a series of large, uncoordinated movements across the Horn after about 1550, following the weakening of the highland state by the Muslim assault.

Shewa under Menelik extended its rule over the Oromo to the south and west (LoC); a 2019 Ethiopian university paper describes this as conquest with European arms, attributing the colonial framing to its authors.
A regional case study states the Shawan conquest of one Oromo group met stiff resistance although the group was defeated in the end.
The Oromo Liberation Front was formed in 1973 (per LoC), dedicated to the liberation of the Oromo nation from what it called Ethiopian colonialism.
The Derg deposed Emperor Haile Selassie (1974 revolution).
EPRDF forces took Addis Ababa; the transitional government was constructed from early July 1991 (OLF took part in the London talks).
The 1995 FDRE Constitution established a federal system and recognised the right of nations to self-determination, including secession.
Abiy Ahmed was sworn in as prime minister; Al Jazeera described him as the first prime minister from the Oromo ethnic group.
Afaan Oromo and three other regional languages became federal working languages alongside Amharic.
